‘The Special Intensive Revision exercise has removed more than 13 crore names from the rolls since June 2025. Over a quarter were claimed dead or duplicated, while most were marked as absent or shifted’ | Photo Credit: The Hindu
For nearly a month, Indians across the country have courted the ire and might of the state over a question no citizen in a democratic nation should have to ask. Their anger stems from the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise which has removed more than 13 crore names from the rolls since June 2025. Over a quarter were claimed dead or duplicated, while most were marked as absent or shifted. At one booth in Delhi’s Bela Estate, officials cut 728 out of 729 voters, citing address proof discrepancies. Who decided that so many names should come off the rolls and on what basis?
While the political answer is being debated on the streets and in Parliament, it is clear that the SIR has changed how a voter’s place on the roll is decided. In 1995, the Supreme Court held that a name already on the roll should be presumed to be there legally. The SIR replaced that presumption with a data-matching exercise. The Election Commission of India (ECI) has relied heavily on software for a public task where a single error costs a citizen their vote.
